pairs.rationale: Matthew tells a person who is fasting to wash and anoint so the fast is not displayed. David washes and anoints after the death that ends his fast, and the servants question that change. The same grooming acts have different relations to fasting; David is not represented as following the instruction to conceal a continuing fast.

Both accounts place Jesus' descent alongside a large crowd. Matthew places the descent after the preceding discourse; Luke places it after the mountain selection of the Twelve and before the ensuing teaching. The comparison preserves the different sequence and does not identify the mountain, level place or crowds as one historical scene.

Jesus requests that food be brought before the ensuing meal in both scenes. Matthew refers back to the five loaves and two fish; John requests some newly caught fish. The crowd meal and shore breakfast, amounts and food origins remain distinct, and neither command is independently attested by the other.

Peter walks upon the waters after Jesus commands him to come; Job describes God alone walking upon the sea as on ground. The particular sea-walking image is shared, while divine sovereignty and the dependent disciple remain distinct. Job does not independently narrate Peter or make him the sole divine walker.

The disciples react to the marriage ruling by saying it is better not to marry. Paul advises unmarried people and widows about remaining as he is, while qualifying the advice where self-control is lacking. This compares particular assessments of unmarried life without converting the disciples' reaction into Jesus' command or erasing Paul's qualifications.

Matthew closes the feast account with many called and few chosen. Luke records a question about few being saved, followed by Jesus' warning that many will seek entry and not be able. Both confront restricted admission despite approach or invitation; Luke is not made a quotation of called/chosen terminology or a statistical salvation rate.

Both warnings associate a coming moral deterioration with damaged love. Matthew explicitly makes increasing lawlessness the cause of love growing cold; Second Timothy describes the last days through wrongdoing and disordered or absent love. The specific causal clause belongs to Matthew and is not inserted into Timothy, nor are the settings assigned one calculated date.

The following addresses identify the meaning of the parable's right/left placement: those at the right are invited to inherit the kingdom, while those at the left are told to depart. This is the same discourse's explicit interpretation of its allocated sides, not an independent sheep-and-goat event or a new meaning for every animal detail.

The later account returns to the centurion and those with him guarding Jesus, describing their response to the earthquake and events. This traces the watchers introduced sitting here into their later narrated testimony. It does not independently repeat the sitting posture or identify each guard personally.

Both scenes associate an overwhelming reaction with an extraordinary appearing figure. Matthew says the guards shook and became like dead men; Daniel describes frightened companions and his own loss of strength and collapse. The participants, their perception and their exact reactions remain distinct; Matthew does not say the guards literally died.

Matthew records a promise to protect the guards from anxiety if their account reaches the governor. Acts reports Herod searching for Peter, examining the guards and ordering them led away for execution. This is a concrete comparison of guard accountability after a missing charge, without importing Herod's sentence into Matthew or claiming a universal Roman custody law.
